# Where the eclipse would have been visible at 9:10 PDT

## Short answer

**At 9:10 a.m. PDT the "ring of fire" was still out over the Pacific Ocean, off the coast
of Oregon — it had not yet reached land anywhere in the United States.** On the map in the
video, 9:10 PDT falls *beyond the top-left (northwest) end of the drawn path*, out in the
water shown west of the Oregon/northern-California coastline. The shadow only made landfall
on the Oregon coast a few minutes later, at roughly 9:13–9:15 a.m. PDT. So the only people
who could have seen annularity at 9:10 PDT were at sea (or in the air) in the eastern North
Pacific, a few hundred miles west-northwest of Oregon, watching a ring-shaped Sun low on
their horizon.

## What the map actually shows

The map appears roughly 8–10 seconds into the video, behind the words "EXPERIENCE THE RING
OF FIRE". It is NASA's path map for the **annular solar eclipse of 14 October 2023**.

- A dark, hatched band labelled **"Annular Solar Eclipse"** runs diagonally across the
  United States from the **northwest (Oregon / northern California) down to the southeast
  (Utah, New Mexico, Texas and the Gulf coast)**.
- Inside the band are faint contour lines labelled **"3 min", "4 min", "5 min"** — the
  duration of annularity.
- Laid along the band is a series of **oval outlines of the Moon's antumbral shadow**, each
  tagged with the local clock time at which the shadow sits in that spot.

Reading the ovals from northwest to southeast, the labels are:

| Oval | Time label | Region it covers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (label clipped by the top of the frame; only "PDT" is legible, next to Medford) | 9:20 PDT (inferred) | Southern Oregon / far northern California — Medford, Klamath Falls |
| 2 | **9:25 PDT** | Northern Nevada — Winnemucca, Elko, Ely |
| 3 | **10:30 MDT** | Southwest/central Utah — Parowan, Richfield, Monticello |
| 4 | **10:35 MDT** | Northwest New Mexico — Farmington, Gallup, Albuquerque, Santa Fe |
| 5 | **10:40 MDT** | Southeast New Mexico — Roswell |
| 6 | **11:45 CDT** | West Texas — Hobbs/Carlsbad toward Midland |

The decisive structural fact is that **the ovals are spaced exactly five minutes apart**:
9:25 PDT = 10:25 MDT, then 10:30, 10:35, 10:40 MDT, then 11:45 CDT = 10:45 MDT. The map is
therefore a timetable — it tells you where the ring of fire was, minute by minute, as it
swept southeast across the country.

## Reading the map backwards to 9:10 PDT

Stepping northwest along the band, five minutes per oval:

- **9:25 PDT** — northern Nevada (Winnemucca / Elko / Ely).
- **9:20 PDT** — the clipped oval on the Oregon–California border (Medford / Klamath Falls /
  Crater Lake area). The video's letterbox crops the numeral off, but its position and the
  five-minute cadence fix it at 9:20.
- **9:15 PDT** — one step further northwest: **western Oregon**, roughly the Eugene–Corvallis
  corridor and the central Oregon coast, where the path makes landfall.
- **9:10 PDT** — one step further northwest again, which lands **off the northwest corner of
  the map, out over the Pacific Ocean west of Oregon**.

The map itself never labels 9:10, and it cannot: at that moment the shadow was not over any
of the territory the map depicts.

## Corroboration from the eclipse itself

This reading matches the published circumstances of the 14 October 2023 eclipse. The annular
phase began at about 16:10 UTC, which is exactly 9:10 a.m. PDT — the Moon's antumbral shadow
touched the Earth at sunrise over the eastern North Pacific and then raced southeast, coming
ashore at the Oregon Dunes / Florence area on the Oregon coast at about 9:13 a.m. PDT
(annularity on the Oregon centreline is usually quoted as beginning ~9:15 a.m. PDT). In other
words, the eclipse was "born" in the Pacific only about three to five minutes before it
reached Oregon. At 9:10 PDT the shadow was travelling at roughly 7,500 mph, so it was on the
order of 300–500 miles (500–800 km) west-northwest of the Oregon shoreline and closing fast.

## Two things worth stating explicitly

1. **This is about annularity, not about seeing *any* eclipse.** The ovals on the map mark
   only the narrow path where the complete ring of fire was visible. A *partial* eclipse was
   already well under way over a very wide area at 9:10 PDT — the partial phases began around
   8:05–8:10 a.m. PDT on the West Coast. So at 9:10 PDT observers across Oregon, Washington,
   California, Nevada, Idaho and much of the rest of the western United States would already
   have seen a bite taken out of the Sun; they simply were not yet seeing the ring.

2. **Nowhere in the contiguous United States had annularity at 9:10 PDT.** If the question is
   "which state?", the honest answer from the map is "none yet — the ocean". Oregon is the
   first state to get it, a handful of minutes later, and the first place the map can actually
   draw an oval on land is the Medford/Klamath Falls area of southern Oregon at 9:20 PDT.

Sources consulted to check the real-world timings:
[Great American Eclipse — October 14, 2023](https://www.greatamericaneclipse.com/october-14-2023),
[NOAA NESDIS — 2023 Annular Solar Eclipse](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/events/2023-annular-solar-eclipse),
[OPB — October's annular eclipse over the US will begin at the Oregon Coast](https://www.opb.org/article/2023/10/03/octobers-annular-eclipse-over-the-us-begins-at-the-oregon-coast/),
[NASA Science — 2023 Annular Eclipse: Where & When](https://science.nasa.gov/eclipses/future-eclipses/eclipse-2023/where-when/).
